item.title: Ozone Hole Reaches Its 2026 Maximum
item.summary: The ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring, but it was not as deep as other large holes on record.
item.page_text:
The ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring, but it was not as deep as other large holes on record.
This story is an update to the Antarctic ozone hole feature in our World of Change series , which documents how Earth changes over months, seasons, and years.
The stratospheric ozone layer protects life on Earth by absorbing ultraviolet light, which damages DNA in plants and animals (including humans) and leads to sunburns and skin cancer. Prior to 1979, scientists had not observed atmospheric ozone concentrations below 220 Dobson Units . But in 1985, British Antarctic Survey scientists using ground-based measurements at Halley Research Station reported that Earth’s natural sunscreen was thinning dramatically over Antarctica each spring. NASA satellite instruments revealed the continental scale of this Antarctic ozone thinning, and it came to be known as the ozone hole.
The data visualizations below shows the ozone hole each year from 1979 through 2026 (no data are available for 1995). The measurements were made from 1979-2004 by the TOMS (NASA’s Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer) instruments on Nimbus-7 and several additional satellites; from 2005-2011 by the OMI (Ozone Monitoring Instrument) on the Aura satellite; from 2012-2025 by the OMPS (Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite; and in 2026 by the OMPS on the NOAA-20 satellite. Red and yellow areas indicate the ozone hole.
As the images show, the word hole isn’t literal; no place is empty of ozone. Scientists use the word hole as a metaphor for the area in which ozone concentrations drop below the historical threshold of 220 Dobson Units . Using this metaphor, they can describe the hole’s area and depth. These maps show the state of the ozone hole each year on the day of maximum depth—the day the lowest ozone concentrations were measured.
The series begins in 1979. The maximum depth of the hole that year was 194 Dobson Units (DU)—not far below the previous historical low. For several years, the maximum depth stayed in the 190s, but then rapidly grew deeper: 173 DU in 1982, 154 in 1983, 124 in 1985. By 1991, a new threshold was passed, as the ozone concentration fell below 100 DU for the first time. Since then, concentrations below 100 DU have become more common. The deepest ozone hole occurred in 1994, when concentrations fell to just 73 DU on September 30.
Records in depth and area have never occurred in the same year (the largest ozone hole occurred in 2006), but the long-term trend in both characteristics is consistent: from 1980 through the early 1990s, the hole rapidly grew in area and depth. In the early years of the 21st century, annual ozone holes roughly stabilized (see NASA Ozone Watch for annual averages). Year-to-year fluctuations in area and depth are caused by variations in stratospheric temperature and circulation. Colder conditions result in a larger area and lower ozone values in the core of the hole.
That was the case in 2026, when an unusually strong Antarctic polar vortex created ideal conditions for ozone depletion over a large area. Measured by its mean size from September 7 to October 13, which is peak ozone depletion season, the 2026 hole was the seventh largest in 48 years of monitoring . However, it was not as deep as other large holes on record. The map at the top of this page shows the hole on September 18, the day of its annual maximum area.
The ozone hole opened the world’s eyes to the global effects of human activity on the atmosphere. Scientists learned that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)—long-lived chemicals that had been used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays since the 1930s—had a dark side. In the layer of the atmosphere closest to Earth (the troposphere), CFCs circulate for decades without degrading or reacting with other chemicals. When they reach the stratosphere, however, their behavior changes. In the upper stratosphere (beyond the protection of the ozone layer), ultraviolet light causes CFCs to break apart, releasing chlorine, a very reactive atom that repeatedly catalyzes ozone destruction .
The global recognition of the destructive potential of CFCs led to the 1987 Montreal Protocol , a treaty phasing out the consumption and production of ozone-depleting chemicals. Scientists estimate that about 80 percent of the chlorine in the stratosphere today comes from human, not natural, sources. Human-produced bromine compounds, which are far less abundant but much more destructive to ozone, also contribute to the Antarctic ozone hole.
Models suggest that the concentration of chlorine and other ozone-depleting substances in the stratosphere will not return to pre-1980 levels until later in the 21st century. In 2018, scientists reported the first direct satellite evidence of ozone recovery, observing a 20 percent decrease in ozone depletion during the Antarctic winter months from 2005 to 2016. In 2019, abnormal weather patterns in the upper atmosphere over Antarctica dramatically limited ozone depletion, leading to the smallest hole since 1982—illustrating the impact of year-to-year variations in the meteorology of the Antarctic stratosphere. Scientists estimate that the Antarctic ozone layer will return to 1980 levels in the 2070s.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using data from NASA Ozone Watch .

item.title: Vega Island's skull-shaped glaciers are losing their "face", and scientists say a warmer ...
item.summary: NASA's Landsat 9 satellite captured the island twice in recent years. The March 2025 image shows it as it typically appears at the start of ...
item.page_text:
From space, Vega Island looks like something staring back at you. Locked in the remote Weddell Sea east of the Antarctic Peninsula, its glaciers, rock outcrops, and moraines trace the unmistakable profile of a grinning skull — a nunatak for an eye socket, a lateral moraine curling into a mouth, the Bahía del Diablo Glacier forming a jawbone.
Satellite images captured in October 2026 show the skull has changed. Snow that typically blankets the island is gone across large stretches, replaced by darker, bare ice. Something about the winter that just passed was different — and the glaciers are showing it.
Vega Island sits in one of the most isolated corners of the Southern Ocean, locked in the Weddell Sea east of the Antarctic Peninsula. From space, it’s hard to look away. A nunatak punches through the ice to form a hollow eye socket, and a lateral moraine curves beneath it like a grinning mouth. The Bahía del Diablo Glacier stretches below as a jawbone. Together, they form a skull profile that faces toward Devil Island, as if keeping watch across the frozen sea.
NASA’s Landsat 9 satellite captured the island twice in recent years. The March 2025 image shows it as it typically appears at the start of austral autumn — snow coating the ice as expected during the region’s wettest month . The October 2026 image tells a different story: large stretches of bare, darker ice exposed where snow should be. The skull’s features remain, but they look rawer, more weathered.
The bare ice in that October 2026 image traces back to the winter that preceded it. Above-average temperatures — particularly in June — are partly responsible, according to glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The exposed ice reflects limited new snow accumulation over winter, a deficit made worse by sublimation and wind scouring. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers,” Pelto said.
In a typical Antarctic winter, fresh snowfall builds a reflective white layer across the ice — one that insulates the surface and shields it from the solar energy arriving with spring. In 2026, that layer was largely absent, leaving bare ice that behaves very differently once the sun returns.
Snow reflects a large proportion of incoming solar radiation back into the atmosphere. Bare, dark ice absorbs significantly more of it . As austral spring lengthens the days and the sun climbs higher, that difference in absorption accelerates surface melt through a self-reinforcing process known as the ice-albedo feedback .
Pelto noted that even modest relief could help. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” he said. His description of what exposure means for the skull’s appearance is precise: “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.” One season of unusual bare-ice conditions is already a meaningful signal — particularly when placed against the longer record.
Scientists have tracked Vega Island’s ice for decades. A 1982 study provided the first comprehensive mapping of the island’s glaciers, drawing on early Landsat imagery, aerial photographs, and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers across four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers .
Of those 29, Bahía del Diablo Glacier has been the most closely watched — monitored continuously since the austral summer of 1998–1999. The data show an overall decline in mass over that period. Satellite imagery from recent decades documents ice loss across multiple other glaciers on the island, with increasing areas of exposed bedrock appearing where ice once held. The bare-ice conditions of October 2026 fit into a pattern of gradual retreat the satellite record has been quietly documenting for years.
Long before any scientist pointed a satellite at Vega Island, it figured into one of Antarctic exploration’s more harrowing chapters. The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901–1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife of the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party eventually split into three groups, each isolated through a brutal winter, and their ship was crushed by pack ice, stranding them further .
Cape Well-met — located on what the skull’s profile would call its forehead — became the site of a joyful spring 1903 reunion between two of those groups. An Argentinean expedition later rescued the survivors. The island that once tested the limits of human endurance is now itself undergoing a slow transformation. The skull’s face, preserved in ice for well over a century, may not look the same in another hundred years.

item.title: Utopian London
item.summary: Today's #30DayMapChallenge is Utopia . There have been lots of pixel-art maps appearing online recently. I covered several of these projects in my recent Pixelate the World post. For today's challenge I thought it might be interesting to create a pixelated map of London – not as it is, but as it might look in an ideal world. Greater London covers approximately 1,591 square kilometres. If each zoomed-in map tile covers roughly 0.15 square kilometres, I would need in the region of 10,600 images to create enough tiles to cover the entire capital. That's a few too many for a simple map challenge, so I decided to create a much smaller map - using just one tile - of Trafalgar Square. My Utopian London map reimagines Trafalgar Square as a greener, more cycle-friendly urban landscape. To create the map I started by feeding an aerial image of Trafalgar Square into Gemini and asking it to transform the scene into pixel art. I also asked it to grass over the roads, plant more trees and introduce dedicated cycle lanes. The result is a more appealing alternative vision of central London. item.title: IRGC Targets Three Oil Tankers in the Strait of Hormuz - Townhall
item.summary: Sentinel-2 satellite imagery shows a large, dark column of smoke rising near the location where NASA FIRMS first detected a thermal anomaly at ...
item.page_text:
The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps claims to have destroyed three oil tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy (IRGC-N) says three vessels that attempted an “unauthorized” transit of the Strait of Hormuz “suffered explosions and fires.” The video it released with the statement shows a column of smoke rising from an intense fire in the distance, taken from a moving vessel. The IRGC has attributed similar incidents to naval mines, a claim disputed by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) who says the recognized primary transit routes are clear of all mines. Nearly every incident reported an attack by unknown projectiles, likely drones and missiles. Attacks on shipping in the region continue to escalate, with the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Center reporting about 10 incidents since November 1st, including at least two in which a seafarer was killed.
Sentinel-2 satellite imagery shows a large, dark column of smoke rising near the location where NASA FIRMS first detected a thermal anomaly at about 6 a.m. UTC today. The imagery comes as Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says three tankers exploded and caught fire this morning along an “unauthorized” route in the Strait of Hormuz.
Satellite images depicted smoke rising from the Strait. Authorities from the United Kingdom had confirmed incidents with two tankers crossing the Strait this morning, but announced that no casualties were sustained by any of the crew.
The renewed action in the Strait follows a strike by U.S. forces against a tanker in the Gulf of Oman that reportedly attempted to violate the blockade against the Islamic Republic of Iran.
CENTCOM forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Nov. 7, after the ship’s civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times. A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, disabling the ship after CENTCOM forces directed the crew to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port. Read the full release online: https://t.co/5wW1LqN1oW

item.page_text:
Isfahan’s judiciary chief said executions of people arrested during the January 2026 protests would continue, after seven protesters were executed in the city.
Asadollah Jafari also said authorities had identified more than 112 people, including some celebrities, over their alleged role in the protests, and had seized or confiscated their property.
He said courts had continued proceedings during holidays and handled some cases quickly, particularly those allegedly involving attacks on police.
The discussion, hosted by Fardad Farahzad, brought together Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior official at the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC); Patrick Clawson, the Morningstar senior fellow at the Washington Institute; and Mohammad Machine-Chian, a senior economist and analyst at Iran International.
“The thing about sanctions, if they’re on the books but not enforced, they only hurt the people,” Bitsoff said, arguing that the current US campaign differed from previous rounds by focusing more heavily on enforcement and the financial intermediaries sustaining Iran’s economy.
Iran faces declining oil revenues alongside damage to its energy infrastructure following the war, raising the prospect of severe economic difficulties during the coming winter, Clawson said.
President Masoud Pezeshkian had acknowledged that Iran could not export oil during the initial blockade, according to Clawson, who said the country subsequently sought alternative routes for limited shipments.
Iran had also relied on oil previously stored aboard vessels and in China, but those reserves were approaching exhaustion, he said.
Damage to natural gas infrastructure could compound the difficulties, potentially forcing greater reliance on mazut, a heavily polluting fuel used for electricity generation.
Iran depends on natural gas for approximately 69 percent of its energy requirements, making disruptions particularly consequential for households and industry, Clawson said.
Machine-Chian estimated that between $21 and $23 billion in export proceeds had not returned to Iran and that the blockade could cost the country another $35 billion in oil revenue.
Hitting financial networks sustaining Iran's leadership
The current campaign differs from previous sanctions because Washington is concentrating on enforcement and the intermediaries sustaining Iran's economy rather than simply announcing additional restrictions, Bitsoff said.
She pointed to restrictions imposed by the United Arab Emirates, measures against Iranian airlines and Turkish action against banks connected to Iranian transactions.
Such measures could influence officials and business figures whose continued support for the Islamic Republic depends on financial privileges and access to international markets.
Earlier sanctions had often pushed legitimate commerce underground while allowing networks connected to the Revolutionary Guards to profit, Bitsoff said.
Machine-Chian described the emergence of wealthy intermediaries, sometimes called sanctions merchants, who benefited from moving Iranian oil and money through opaque arrangements.
Those networks subsequently became obstacles to negotiations and economic normalization because their commercial interests depended on maintaining the existing system, he said.
Machine-Chian distinguished between sanctions that impose prolonged hardship without producing results and measures designed to achieve specific objectives within a foreseeable period.
The loss of the UAE, Machine-Chian added, as a major commercial and financial intermediary has further complicated Iran's position.
Dubai previously provided an important channel for Iranian transactions, but restrictions have forced businesses to seek alternatives through Turkey, Pakistan and Afghanistan, Machine-Chian said.
Those routes, he said, have limited capacity and cannot quickly replace the financial infrastructure previously available through the Emirates.
China and regional allies face financial constraints
China remains Iran's principal oil customer, but its commercial relationship offers fewer advantages to the Islamic Republic than commonly assumed, Bitsoff said.
Independent Chinese refineries purchase Iranian crude at substantial discounts, while payments in yuan often remain in China and are largely available for purchasing Chinese goods.
Major Chinese banks generally avoid Iranian transactions, leaving smaller intermediaries to facilitate much of the remaining trade, she said.
The blockade also allows Washington to restrict Iranian oil exports without directly confronting major Chinese financial institutions, Clawson said.
Targeting those institutions could provoke Chinese retaliation affecting broader US economic interests.
The financial pressure is also affecting Iran's regional allies.
Hezbollah has struggled to maintain basic financial obligations and social support programs since the blockade began, Bitsoff said.
Machine-Chian argued that Iran's relationships with allied armed groups had become increasingly transactional, making continued financial assistance essential to sustaining their loyalty.
Political survival and prospects for negotiations
Despite the mounting pressure, the panelists differed over whether the Islamic Republic would ultimately accept Washington's demands.
Economic hardship alone was unlikely to persuade Iran's leadership to abandon its objectives, Bitsoff said.
Instead sustained pressure could influence members of the security apparatus whose loyalty depends on salaries, privileges and expectations of continued stability.
Clawson considered negotiated concessions possible, pointing to previous occasions when Iran reversed positions it had presented as nonnegotiable.
He suggested Iran could accept a three-year suspension of uranium enrichment, particularly because its facilities had been damaged and were not operational.
